tracks.title: Investing basics
tracks.summary: Sample lessons that explain what you are actually buying.

lessons.title: What is a stock?
lessons.summary: A plain explanation of what a share of a company represents.

blocks.text: A small piece of a company
A stock is a share of ownership in a company. When you buy a stock you buy a small piece of that business, and its price moves with how the market values the company.

items: Share prices change every day as buyers and sellers trade.
You can lose part or all of the money you put in.
Some companies also pay dividends, a share of their profits.

blocks.text: Sample lesson. Real lessons are written and reviewed by the AskVest team before launch.

questions.prompt: What does buying a stock give you?

options.text: A small share of ownership in the company

questions.explanation: A stock is a share of ownership. It is not a loan and it does not promise any return.

questions.prompt: Can the value of a stock go down after you buy it?

options.text: No, the price only rises over time

questions.explanation: Share prices change constantly and can fall as well as rise.

options.text: A share of company profits paid to shareholders
A fee charged by the exchange

questions.explanation: Some companies share part of their profits with shareholders as dividends.

lessons.title: What is an ETF?
lessons.summary: How exchange traded funds bundle many investments together.

blocks.text: An ETF, or exchange traded fund, holds a basket of many stocks or other assets. Buying one ETF gives you a small piece of everything in that basket.

items: ETFs often track an index, a sector or a theme.
They spread your money across many holdings at once.
They still lose value when their holdings fall.

blocks.text: Spreading money lowers single-company risk but does not remove market risk.

questions.prompt: What does an ETF typically hold?
questions.explanation: An ETF bundles many holdings into one tradable fund.

questions.prompt: Does buying an ETF remove the risk of losing money?

options.text: No, it spreads risk but losses are still possible

questions.explanation: Diversification lowers exposure to any single holding but markets can still fall.

questions.prompt: What does it mean that an ETF tracks an index?

options.text: Its value follows a published basket of assets
It is managed by the government

questions.explanation: Index-tracking ETFs aim to mirror the performance of a defined basket.

tracks.title: Investing safely
tracks.summary: Sample lessons on risk, ownership and costs.

lessons.title: Risk and diversification
lessons.summary: Why spreading money matters and what risk really means.

blocks.text: Risk means the chance that an investment loses money. Prices move for many reasons, and past gains do not predict future results.

items: Putting all money in one company concentrates your risk.
Spreading across many holdings lowers, but never removes, risk.
Only invest money you can afford to leave invested for a long time.

blocks.text: This lesson has no quiz. Marking it complete counts as learning activity.

lessons.title: What you actually own
lessons.summary: Holding a token is not the same as owning the share.

blocks.text: A token that tracks a stock is a digital record managed by an issuer. Holding it is not the same as holding the share itself: the rights, backing and exit options depend on the issuer's terms.

items: Read the issuer's disclosures before you buy.
Check who holds the backing and how redemption works.
A price can track the share while your rights differ.

blocks.text: Always read the token disclosure carefully. It explains exactly what you hold.

questions.prompt: Is holding a token that tracks a stock the same as owning the share?

options.text: Yes, they are identical in every way
No, rights and backing depend on the issuer's terms

questions.explanation: A tracking token is a claim managed by an issuer, not the share itself.

questions.prompt: Where should you check what a token actually gives you?
questions.explanation: Disclosures state backing, rights, fees and exit options in writing.

questions.prompt: Why does a token's price sometimes differ from the share's price?

options.text: Because demand, fees and settlement differ
Because the share has stopped trading

questions.explanation: Supply, demand, fees and market hours can push a token away from its reference price.

lessons.title: Fees and costs
lessons.summary: Small costs add up and change what you keep.

blocks.text: Costs are part of every trade
Buying and selling usually costs money: trading fees, spreads and fund expenses. These costs repeat and reduce what you keep over time.

items: Fees are often a percentage of the amount traded.
A fund's ongoing expenses come out of its return.
Compare the total cost, not just the headline price.

blocks.text: AskVest practice mode shows a simulated fee so you can see how costs work.

questions.prompt: Why do small fees matter over time?

options.text: They repeat on every trade and reduce returns

questions.explanation: Repeated costs compound and leave less money invested.

options.text: The difference between buy and sell prices

questions.explanation: The spread is the gap between what buyers pay and sellers receive.

questions.prompt: What should you compare when choosing between similar funds?
questions.explanation: Ongoing expenses and trading costs determine what you actually keep.
